title: State Department Proposes Requiring Parents to Prove Citizenship for Children's Passports
excerpt: Draft guidance would require all parents to submit proof of citizenship or immigration status when applying for their children's U.S. passports, as the Trump administration moves to enforce its narrower birthright citizenship order.
body:
• The U.S. State Department has drafted guidance requiring parents to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status when applying for children's passports.
  • The proposal would implement Trump's August 6 executive order targeting "birth tourism" after the Supreme Court struck down his broader birthright citizenship order in a 6-3 ruling.
  • Currently, parents only need to prove parentage and show photo ID — supporting citizenship documentation is not required.
  • Lawyers have filed class-action lawsuits asking federal judges to block the new order before it takes effect.

The U.S. State Department has proposed a significant change to the passport application process that could affect millions of immigrant families: requiring all parents and legal guardians to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status when applying for passports for their U.S.-born children.

The draft guidance, first reported by Reuters on September 1, offers the most detailed look yet at how the federal government plans to implement President Donald Trump's August 6 executive order — his second attempt at restricting birthright citizenship after the Supreme Court struck down his initial, broader effort.

What the New Rules Would Require

Under the proposed changes, parents applying for a child's passport would need to submit documentation proving their own status. U.S. citizen parents could provide a valid passport or birth certificate. Non-citizen parents would need to present evidence such as an I-94 arrival/departure form or a lawful permanent residency card (green card).

The government would use this information to determine whether the child falls under the categories outlined in Executive Order 14418, which would deny citizenship to children born in the U.S. when neither parent is a citizen and at least one parent is a foreign government employee, is engaged in fraud or a commercial transaction to obtain citizenship, or is classified as an "alien enemy."

Currently, parents whose children were born in the U.S. only need to prove their parentage and present photo identification. While the application form asks whether the parent is a U.S. citizen, no supporting documentation is required.

"President Trump has been unequivocal that this Administration will protect the meaning and value of American citizenship, full stop, and that includes making sure our passport adjudication process fully reflects that standard."

— Tommy Pigott, State Department Spokesman

A Narrower Order After Supreme Court Defeat

The proposal follows a turbulent legal battle over birthright citizenship. Trump's initial executive order, signed in January 2025, would have limited automatic citizenship at birth to children with at least one parent who was a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident. The Supreme Court struck it down in a 6-3 decision in Trump v. Barbara on June 30, 2026, ruling that it violated the Citizenship Clause of the 14th Amendment.

The August 6 order takes a narrower approach, specifically targeting what the administration calls "birth tourism" — the practice of women traveling to the United States to give birth so their children obtain automatic citizenship. Unlike the initial order, this directive carves out specific categories of non-citizen parents rather than broadly excluding all non-citizens and non-permanent residents.

What This Means for Indian Families

For the estimated 2.7 million Indian immigrants living in the United States, the proposed rules add a new layer of documentation requirements to an already complex process. Families on H-1B visas, L-1 transfers, or other work-based visas would need to gather and submit their immigration paperwork when applying for their U.S.-born children's passports — a process that until now required only proof of parentage.

While the narrower categories in the current order may not directly affect most Indian families on employment-based visas, immigration attorneys warn that the documentation requirement itself creates friction and uncertainty, particularly for families already navigating lengthy green card backlogs that can stretch decades for Indian-born applicants.

Legal Challenges Ahead

The new order faces its own legal challenges. Lawyers pursuing class-action lawsuits on behalf of families affected by the initial order have asked two federal judges to block the latest directive. At a hearing on August 29 in Greenbelt, Maryland, U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman expressed skepticism about what she called Trump's "unprecedented order" and allowed plaintiffs to revise their lawsuit to consider whether to issue an injunction.

Justice Department attorneys have argued that blocking the order would be premature, since federal agencies had not yet issued public guidance on implementation — the very guidance the State Department has now drafted.

The outcome of these legal challenges will determine whether the proposed passport requirements ever take effect, with broader implications for how the United States defines and administers citizenship rights for children born on American soil.
nri_angle: Indian families on H-1B and other work visas would face new documentation requirements when applying for their U.S.-born children's passports, adding bureaucratic friction amid already lengthy green card backlogs.
